title: Starting a fire when everything is wet (rain or snow)
asks: how to start a fire in the rain
everything is wet how do i make a fire
how to find dry wood after rain
start a fire with wet wood
how to build a fire on snow
will a ferro rod work when wet
how 2 lite a fire wen its raining
soaked and cold, need a fire fast, all the wood is wet, over
answer: Use standing or leaning dead wood. It is usually dry even in rainy climates, because its vertical position sheds most rain.

Split wood to get at the inner wood. The inner wood of dead branches and small-diameter trees is the driest, and split wood burns faster and hotter than pieces covered by bark, which collects moisture.
Wood less than 3 inches in diameter and about 1 to 2 feet long can be split with a strong fixed-blade knife, using a sturdy forearm-sized branch to drive the knife down the wood along the grain.
For kindling, look for small dead branches low to the ground on the underside of conifers.
Build on a dry base, a flat piece of wood or nonporous rock, to keep tinder and kindling off the wet ground.
Dry damp natural tinder before use by storing it between layers of your clothing.
Use a sufficient amount of tinder: it must make a flame hot enough to ignite the kindling.
A metal match is not affected by wet conditions, and good sparks from it can compensate for some moisture in the tinder.
Matches must be waterproof and stored in a waterproof container. Damp matches burn weaker or not at all.
Use a tepee fire lay: tinder and a few sticks of kindling arranged in the shape of a cone. This type of fire burns well even with wet wood.
Fuel does not have to be completely dry if the fire is established well enough to dry it before it burns. The more moisture in the fuel, the more white smoke.
As a last resort, green wood can be made to burn if it is finely split and mixed evenly with dry, dead wood.

In deep snow where the soil cannot be reached, build the fire on a base of green logs stacked in two layers, the top layer perpendicular to the bottom, so the coals do not melt a hole through the snow pack.
Pick a fire site that is protected from the wind and away from snow-laden trees.
warnings: Do not use porous rock as a base, and remove it from the fire site. Porous rocks contain water and can explode when heated.
Do not pour highly flammable liquids on an existing fire. Even a smoldering fire can make them explode and cause serious burns.

quotes.text: Standing or leaning dead wood is usually dry even in rainy climates as its vertical position sheds most rain.

The inner wood of dead branches and small diameter trees is the driest because it is not exposed to the weather. Wood that is split to expose the inner wood grains burns faster and hotter than wood pieces that are covered by bark which naturally protects trees from fire and collects moisture. Wood less than 3 inches in diameter and approximately 1 to 2 feet in length can easily be split using a strong fixed blade survival knife and a sturdy forearm sized branch. The branch is used to drive the knife down the length of the wood along the grain.

Small branches low to the ground on the underside of coniferous trees that are dead from lack of sun (a single branch often has all three sizes of kindling on it that simply need to be broken down for use).

The base is a flat piece of material, usually wood or a nonporous rock (porous rocks contain water and, when heated, can explode). The base is used to keep moisture susceptible tinder and kindling off the wet ground and provides a clear area to skillfully ignite tinder.
Porous rock is removed from the fire site, which is at risk of exploding from the heat of the fire.
Isolated persons can procure natural tinder, when damp, and store it between layers of clothing to use heat radiated by the body to dry it prior to use.
A sufficient amount of tinder must be used to generate a hot enough flame to ignite kindling in the next phase of fire building.
Metal matches are reliable and not effected by wet or dry conditionals, cold or hot weather, evaporation or age, and do not malfunction.
Good sparks from a metal match burn hot, fast, and can compensate for some moisture in tinder.
Ensure that these matches are waterproof, stored in a waterproof container, and have a striker pad.
Matches can quickly become damp due to their size and exposed wood grain. When damp, their effectiveness is reduced causing them to burn weaker or not at all.

Tepee fires are made by arranging the tinder and a few sticks of kindling in the shape of a tepee or cone. The center can be lighted after the structure is built or the structure can be built around a small fire. As the tepee burns, the outside logs will fall inward, feeding the fire. This type of fire burns well even with wet wood.

Unlike tinder and kindling, fire fuel does not have to be kept completely dry if the fire is established well enough to dry the damp fuel before burning. However, the more moisture fuel contains the more white smoke the fire will produced as it burns it off.
As a last resort green wood, which is found almost anywhere, can be made to burn if finely split and mixed evenly with dry, dead wood.
In deep snow where the soil cannot be reached, green logs are used as a base to build the fire on to prevent the coals from melting a hole through the snow pack and away from isolated persons.
Pieces are stacked in two layers, the top being perpendicular to the bottom to a size that contains the entirety of the intended fire.
Fire sites should meet the following basic criteria:
Protected from the wind.
Away from snow laden trees.
Highly flammable liquids should not be poured on an existing fire. Even a smoldering fire can cause liquids to explode and cause serious burns.

All lines rest on ATP 3-50.21 ch. 5 and keep their meaning: standing/leaning dead wood is dry, split to the inner wood, baton-split wood under 3 in and 1-2 ft long, dead lower conifer branches for kindling, dry base off wet ground, dry damp tinder between clothing layers, enough tinder, metal match unaffected by wet and good sparks compensate for some moisture, waterproof matches and damp matches burn weak, tepee lay burns well with wet wood, damp fuel once established (more white smoke), green wood finely split and mixed with dry as a last resort, two-layer green-log base on deep snow, site protected from wind and away from snow-laden trees. Warnings (porous rock, flammable liquids) correct. No contradicting kit text found (TC 21-3's 'sticks laid out like the spokes of a wheel' is another lay, not a conflict). All asks answered, including the ferro-rod-when-wet ask. Optional: TC 21-3 ch. 7 'Carry candles... help start fires' would help the 'need a fire fast' ask.
